content.title: About
content.content: Quail are small game birds from the pheasant family, farmed worldwide. Cooked quail meat is known for its delicate flavor, slight sweetness, and tender texture. It is served whole, as fillets, or cut into pieces, using methods such as roasting, grilling, pan‑frying, or braising.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Quail can fly up to 3,000 m altitude, but in culinary production they are usually raised in controlled environments.
The meat is protein‑dense, providing about 24 g of protein per 100 g.
In Japan, quail is often served as "tenkatsu" – breaded and deep‑fried pieces.
Quail eggs are 5‑6 times smaller than chicken eggs yet contain higher levels of vitamin B12.
Ancient Romans considered quail a delicacy, serving them with honey and exotic spices.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: High‑quality protein supports muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with beef or pork, quail meat contains less saturated fat, making it suitable for lean‑diet plans.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Provides niacin, vitamin B6 and riboflavin, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Contains iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood health and bone structure.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Selenium and vitamin E help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Bird allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to poultry, including quail.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: People with gout or elevated uric acid should limit consumption.

items.title: Cholesterol
items.content: While low in fat, quail liver is relatively high in cholesterol.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Quail can be roasted whole, grilled, braised in sauce, or pan‑seared as fillets. They pair well with herbs, citrus, honey, or soy sauce. Fillets are convenient for salads, pastas, and rice dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh quail should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen quail can be stored at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw in the fridge, not at room temperature, before cooking.
